narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school placed you far below the average student who was accepted (who typically ranked around the 6th decile). These consistently low academic standings within your own school signaled to the model a high risk that you would struggle to pass the bar.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, and it worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the average of accepted students (37.18), so it provided a modest pull toward the possibility of passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not nearly strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly. Improving your class rank in future years or gaining targeted bar-prep experience could substantially improve your chances in a future application.
